newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWIMMING-ASTHMA TREATMENTS NO HELP FOR SWIMMERS.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-ASTHMA TREATMENTS NO HELP FOR SWIMMERS.

text.p: Swimmers who take asthma treatments in the hope of improving their performance are wasting their time, doctors said at a medical conference on Sunday.

They said data showed a higher proportion of swimmers than any other athletes use inhaled steroids and beta stimulant bronchodilators, the mainstay of asthma treatments which dilate the airways, making breathing easier.

"They may be thought to benefit by improving ventilation and lung capacity but it is really not very likely that they do," Duncan Empey, consultant physician from London's Royal Hospitals NHS Trust, said during the conference organised by swimming's governing body FINA.

"There is no evidence to show this but, like many things that athletes take, if they believe this is of some benefit to them then they will take it. One would be surprised if they would make any difference other than a psychological one," he said.

Under international rules laid down in 1984, such treatments are acceptable for competitors with asthma as long as they are inhaled and are not taken orally or by injection, and are also declared to officials.

Successful international swimmers with asthma include U.S. Olympic gold medallist Tom Dolan and Australian swimming legend Dawn Fraser, while U.S. swimmer Rick Demont was disqualified from the 1972 games for using drugs.
However officials are finding that non-asthmatic swimmers are taking such treatments and FINA says it is constantly monitoring the list of acceptable treatments.
Amendments were made in 1992 when Clembuterol, which has anabolic effects and is used to make animals more muscular, was struck off the list.
Empey said the steroid inhalers now used were very low dosage. "It would never have any effect on your muscles but this is partly why alarm bells ring in doping circles," he said.
The proportion of swimmers who declare themselves to be asthmatic is higher than in the general population.
In most countries about 10 percent of children and five percent of adults are asthmatic, FINA medical committee member Mohammed Koudiri told the conference.
But fellow committee member Bengt Eriksson said 30 percent of top swimmers were asthmatic.
Eriksson told Reuters the high proportion could be partly due to the fact that swimming attracts more asthmatics than outdoor, strenuous sports like football or athletics.
He said swimmers who suffer hay fever or chest tightness from chlorine inhalation could be viewed as borderline cases and benefit from the occasional use of asthma treatments.
A third group of swimmers do not suffer from asthma but hope using asthma drugs will enhance their performance. "But it is very debatable that they get any advantage," Eriksson said.
